intro: In the fourth movement of Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique, the artist dreams that he is marching to his own execution. A clarinet plays a few bars representing the beloved before the whole orchestra cuts it off.

sections.label: Intro · Timpani and stopped horns
sections.mNote: Soft timpani strokes with pizzicato basses before the march begins.

sections.label: A · Descending bass theme, G minor
sections.mNote: Cellos and double basses play the G minor march theme.

sections.label: B · March theme in B♭, winds and brass
sections.mNote: Winds and brass play the second theme.

sections.label: A′ · G minor, percussion
sections.mNote: The descending theme returns; percussion joins the crescendo.

sections.label: C · Clarinet, the beloved’s melody
sections.mNote: The beloved’s melody returns alone on the clarinet.

sections.label: Coda · Orchestral blow and G major chords
sections.mNote: An orchestral blow, plucked strings, then G major chords.

relations.label: The major-key march returns
relations.basis: The march’s second theme returns with a more active accompaniment, rather than an exposition restart; this agrees with the major-key march region in the listening notes and the structural account at https://human.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Music/Ethnomusicology/Resonances_-_Engaging_Music_in_its_Cultural_Context_(Morgan-Ellis_Ed.)/02%3A_Music_for_Storytelling/06%3A_Stories_without_Words/6.02%3A_Hector_Berlioz_-_Fantastical_Symphony. CENS diagonal mean 0.955, sustained 41 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 41.5 s (cache/form/berlioz-fantastique-march.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Opening, timpani and stopped horns
cues.text: Timpani begin softly, struck with sponge-headed sticks. Stopped horns enter above plucked cellos and basses. Berlioz’s programme described an opium-dazed musician who dreams that he has murdered his beloved and is being led to execution.
cues.evidence: Movement IV, bars 1–16, Michel Austin’s score transcription: http://www.hberlioz.com/scosupp/symfantas4.pdf . Berlioz’s programme, 1845, part IV: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Descending march, cellos and basses
cues.text: Cellos and double basses play the descending tune of the opening march in unison, over a pizzicato accompaniment in the upper strings. The tune moves down through G minor, stopping and starting between sharp orchestral replies.
cues.evidence: Movement IV, descending march from bar 17; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 3–10, including unison low strings and pizzicato accompaniment.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second march, B♭ major
cues.text: The second march is in B♭ major. Woodwinds and brass play its square, emphatic tune over the strings and timpani.
cues.evidence: Movement IV, second march from bar 62, Michel Austin’s score transcription. Berlioz’s programme describes the procession’s alternation between sombre and ceremonious passages.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Paris, 1830
cues.text: Habeneck conducted the first performance at the Paris Conservatoire on 5 December 1830, after only two rehearsals. The march overwhelmed the audience. In his Mémoires Berlioz recorded its success and the failure of the countryside movement to make an impression.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, Mémoires, chapter 31, on the première, two rehearsals and the march’s reception: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm

cues.title: Return of the march in G minor
cues.text: The descending march returns in G minor, carried by bassoons and low strings. The timpani are played with wooden sticks, and bass drum and cymbals join.
cues.evidence: Movement IV, return and crescendo following the second march; the score specifies wooden timpani sticks and adds bass drum and cymbals. Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 22–34.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Composition of the march
cues.text: Berlioz wrote in his Mémoires that he composed the Marche au supplice in a single night. The slow countryside movement of the same symphony had taken him more than three weeks. He went on revising both, and the other movements, for several years.
cues.evidence: Berlioz, Mémoires, chapter 26 (“La Marche au supplice, au contraire, fut écrite en une nuit”, with the three weeks on the Scène aux champs and years of revision): https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/M%C3%A9moires_de_Hector_Berlioz/26

cues.title: Solo clarinet, the beloved’s melody
cues.text: The march stops and a solo clarinet plays, marked dolce assai ed appassionato — very sweetly and passionately. It begins the beloved’s melody in G major, unaccompanied, in bars 164–168. Berlioz’s programme calls the phrase a final thought of love.
cues.evidence: Movement IV, bars 164–168, Michel Austin’s score transcription, p. 35. The clarinet is unaccompanied after the orchestral release; Berlioz’s programme calls the phrase a final thought of love.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Execution and closing chords
cues.text: A full-orchestra chord cuts off the clarinet. Two short pizzicato notes follow, then the drums roll and the movement ends on full chords in G major.
cues.evidence: Movement IV, bars 169–178, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 36–37: orchestral interruption, pizzicato notes and G-major close. Programme, part IV: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Cellos and basses begin the march
transitions.to: A · Descending bass theme, G minor
transitions.how: Soft timpani and stopped horns lead to an orchestral chord in G minor. Cellos and double basses then play the descending march tune together, bowed. Violins and violas play the accompaniment pizzicato.
transitions.evidence: Movement IV, bars 1–24; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 1–4: http://www.hberlioz.com/scosupp/symfantas4.pdf

transitions.title: The march in B♭ major
transitions.from: A · Descending bass theme, G minor
transitions.to: B · March theme in B♭, winds and brass
transitions.how: The bassoon line and strings diminish. Low brass and timpani prepare the new march, which opens in B♭ major. Flutes, oboes, clarinets, horns and trumpets play the tune above sharply marked strings. The two-beat tread continues.
transitions.evidence: Movement IV, bars 53–69, especially the bassoon passage and preparation at bars 57–61, followed by the B♭-major march.

transitions.title: The bass tune returns in minor
transitions.from: B · March theme in B♭, winds and brass
transitions.how: The B♭ major march thins to plucked strings and wind phrases. G minor returns, and bassoons and low strings play the descending tune. Their crescendo brings the brass back in and adds bass drum, cymbals and timpani played with hard wooden sticks.
transitions.evidence: Movement IV, return following the B♭-major march and its repetition; Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 22–30.

transitions.title: Clarinet enters with the idée fixe
transitions.how: In bars 163–168 a rising orchestral flourish breaks off. The bass instruments stop, and the clarinet begins the idée fixe alone in G major, pianissimo, marked dolce assai ed appassionato. Its long held notes replace the clipped march rhythm.
transitions.evidence: Movement IV, bars 163–168; Michel Austin’s score transcription, p. 35. The solo’s dramatic meaning is given in Berlioz’s programme.

transitions.title: Orchestral chord cuts off the clarinet
transitions.to: Coda · Orchestral blow and G major chords
transitions.how: The clarinet’s phrase ends under a fortissimo chord from the full orchestra. The strings then play two short pizzicato notes. Timpani rolls and chords in the wind and brass follow and make the close in G major. Berlioz’s programme calls the interruption the fatal stroke.
transitions.evidence: Movement IV, bars 169–178, Michel Austin’s score transcription, pp. 36–37; programme, part IV: http://www.hberlioz.com/Scores/fantasf.htm

source.title: Berlioz, Symphonie fantastique, full score (Hector Berlioz Werke, Ser. I, Bd. 1, Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, 1900, ed. Malherbe and Weingartner)
source.locator: IV. Marche au supplice, printed pp. 76–96: timpani opening, descending G-minor tune, B♭-major march and final clarinet recollection. The tuba symbol shows the two low-brass parts.

timeline.note: Sponge-headed timpani and stopped horns begin the march; bassoons join above plucked cellos and basses.
Clarinets, brass and timpani join the low strings in a crescendo to a fortissimo chord.
Cellos and basses play the descending tune in unison; violins and violas play the accompaniment pizzicato.
Strings play the descending tune; the orchestra follows with fortissimo chords.
Winds and brass play the B♭-major march above strings and timpani.
Plucked strings, low brass and timpani play the march’s quieter phrases.
The B♭-major tune returns to winds and brass, with quick figures in the strings.
Plucked strings and a short woodwind trill quieten the procession.
Bassoons and low strings play the returning G-minor tune beneath quick wind figures.
Wooden timpani sticks, bass drum and cymbals join the full orchestra.
The solo clarinet plays the beloved’s melody; the rest of the orchestra stops.
The orchestra cuts the clarinet off; plucked strings, drum rolls and G-major chords follow.

quote.source: Berlioz, Mémoires, chapter XVIII, recalling the Paris performances of September 1827; our translation

composer.background:
When the young Hector Berlioz read aloud the death of Dido, his voice failed him. His father closed the book and said that he was tired, so the boy did not have to explain his tears. Berlioz recorded the kindness in his Mémoires. Louis Berlioz was a doctor in La Côte-Saint-André, between Lyon and Grenoble, and taught his son Latin, history and geography. He expected Hector to follow him into medicine. The boy learnt the flute and guitar, studied maps of distant islands and was deeply moved by the story of Virgil’s abandoned queen.

In 1821 he went to Paris to study medicine. His first visit to the dissecting room at the Pitié hospital, he later wrote, ended with a flight through a window. On the second visit he managed perfectly well. Music was the more durable obstacle. He heard Salieri’s Les Danaïdes at the Opéra and began singing its airs over the cadavers. At the Conservatoire library he copied and memorised Gluck’s scores. His father argued, threatened and withheld support. Hector took composition lessons with Jean-François Le Sueur.
